content: 1. The Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory – Computer Adaptive Test (PEDI-CAT), specifically the Mobility Scaled Score, demonstrated increased scores among all participants. This indicates that power mobility training effectively improved mobility in children with multiple, severe impairments. 2. Verbal mediation was observed to enhance performance in wheelchair drills among adults with right cerebrovascular accidents (CVA). It helped participants achieve safe and independent performance, maintain correct task sequencing during post-tests, and reduce errors. 3. Both verbal mediation and non-verbal mediation slightly reduced the time required to complete wheelchair drills from pre-test to post-test among adults with right CVA. 4. The Adapted Powered Mobility Program and the Smart Wheelchair Mobility Training Program (SWMTP) significantly improved driving skills and positively impacted psychosocial outcomes in children with cerebral palsy. 5. Peer-led, community-based manual wheelchair training programs significantly improved the confidence of adult manual wheelchair users in performing wheelchair maintenance and instructing others in maintenance tasks. 6. Adults with chronic stroke and severe arm impairments showed significant improvements in competence when learning to drive a bimanual propulsion wheelchair over six training sessions. However, there were no significant changes in their perception of effort or usefulness. 7. The Wheelchair Skills Training Program (WSTP) was found to be effective and enjoyable, with participants mastering advanced skills such as ascending and descending curbs, navigating grassy hills, and performing wheelies. 8. Peer-led wheelchair training programs, such as Wheel See U, improved the overall quality of life for older adult manual wheelchair users. Participants reported increased independence, confidence, and social connectedness. 9. Active rehabilitation programs for individuals with spinal cord injuries significantly improved personal function constructs of the Moorong Self-Efficacy Scale (MSES). However, there were no significant changes in the total MSES score or in general and social constructs. 10. Health professionals in Ireland reported a lack of skills and confidence in providing formal training for advanced wheelchair mobility skills. They expressed a desire for opportunities to develop these skills through self-directed learning, workshops, and clinical seminars. 11. In the USA, therapists often receive minimal training in seating and mobility, leading to inexperienced professionals assisting consumers. This has implications for technology abandonment, wasted funding, and delays in equipment provision. 12. The National Registry of Rehabilitation Technology Suppliers (NRRTS) is preparing Rehabilitation Technology Suppliers (RTSs) for credentialing. This initiative aims to help consumers identify qualified service providers and support RTSs in billing for clinical services.
